title: PREDICT (Precision Medicine, Education, Data Informatics and Community Translation) Institute
text:
Modified Public Health Relevance Statement

Public Health Relevance Section

The purpose of the Precision Medicine, Education, Data Informatics, and Community Translation (PREDICT) Institute is to serve as a holistic and replicable framework for the utilization of electronic health data and community translation to affect the decision-making process to improve health outcomes. The PREDICT Institute will extend the technical research exchange (TREX) program at Xavier to include training of current and future researchers on health informatics best practices. The use of population health and bioinformatics data will demonstrate their value as useful tools in collective approaches required to improve health outcomes.

title: Designing addressable proteoliposomes by using viral transmembrane proteins and biomimetic cell-free synthesis techniques.
text:
This research fellowship aims to design a useful tool for both gaining fundamental knowledge of
viral protein-cell membrane interactions and addressing current challenges in targeted drug-
delivery, especially those associated with carrier (delivery vehicle) -cell receptor specificity. By
developing adapted cell-free protein synthesis techniques, we intend to construct user-defined
proteoliposomes whose composition can mirror an exterior viral surface, used towards either
furthering our understanding of virus ligand-host cell interactions or repurposed for targeted
therapies exploiting the native fidelity of virus membrane proteins and for their respective cellular
receptors.

title: Electrical Mapping Signatures of Adverse Structural and Functional Remodeling in Ventricular Arrhythmia
text:
This translational research applies cutting-edge bioengineering techniques to better understand and
characterize the mechanisms of ventricular arrhythmias, which remain the most common cause of sudden
death in patients with heart failure. Novel analysis of the interplay between structural and electrical
abnormalities of the heart will provide actionable classifications of ventricular arrhythmia substrate for therapy
and future study.

title: Antigen Specific T cells
text:
We have developed a “personalized” medicine to treat patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) to prevent
relapse after bone marrow transplant (BMT) by taking immune cells (T-cells) from donor blood and engineering
them to kill leukemia. This project will test whether T cells specific for multiple tumor proteins +/- engineered with
a novel chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) can be generated and infused to prevent relapse after BMT. We believe
that this novel approach will be safe and effective therapy for patients with AML and ultimately for other cancers.

title: University of Wisconsin Prostate SPORE
text:
Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men and a source of significant morbidity and mortality (>30,000
deaths annually). This project will combine our cutting-edge basic science discoveries with clinical (surgical,
medical and radiation oncologists) expertise to exploit novel observations that will improve outcomes and quality
of life for patients with this disease. Using state-of-the-art imaging, bioinformatics and novel pathology resources
we will develop new and exploit new diagnostic approaches and treatments that will change the way prostate
cancer is managed.

title: Discovery and anti-tumor activity of the first antagonists targeting human Sonic Hedgehog autoprocessing
text:
Aberrant biosynthesis of human Sonic hedgehog (Hh) proteins in adult tumors results in a pro-
growth survival signal that can spur tumor cell proliferation, invasiveness and chemoresistance.
Here we pursue the first small molecules to specifically block Hh protein autoprocessing, a key
step in the biosynthesis of these oncogenic effector proteins. We hypothesize that the cell-
permeable small molecules discovered here will show anti-cancer activity against human
myeloma and colon cancer cells, which we will test experimentally to establish the groundwork
for a new class of targeted anti-cancer therapeutics.

title: Fluorescence lifetime tomography for the longitudinal quantification of B cell dynamics during immunotherapy treatment.
text:
lmmunotherapy is a promising new approach for cancer treatment, but only a fraction of patients respond to
treatment, with a majority experiencing drug related side effects. Current screening methods for
immunotherapy biomarkers rely on biopsy, which is invasive and does not always provide an accurate readout
of biomarker status in whole tumors. This proposal will develop a whole-body optical imaging technique that
can quantify biomarkers non-invasively, thereby enabling the efficient development of new combination
treatments and more accurate screening for predictive biomarkers, potentially saving non-responders from
ineffective treatments and life-threatening effects.
Project Narrative

title: A Multi-Scale Study of Antimicrobial Peptide Action Beyond Steady-State Growth
text:
Antimicrobial resistance is a growing global health threat, and antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising
alternative to traditional antibiotics. However, AMP efficacy is poorly understood in complex bacterial
environments, such as biofilms, high-density colonies, and nutrient-deprived cells, which are common in real
infections. This project will investigate AMP action across these conditions using microfluidic models, single-
cell analysis, and RNA-sequencing, ultimately guiding the development of next-generation AMPs with improved
therapeutic potential.

title: Molecular Virology Core
text: To understand the critical factors that negatively impact gene therapy for hemophilia A, our program will investigate the key problems associated with AAV vector production and design, factor VIII (FVIII) expression, and role of the immune system. Proposed gene transfer studies critically rely on strict control of vector composition and thorough characterization of vector properties before and after vector administration. Unfortunately, in-depth characterization of vectors is stymied by the lack of knowledge of some of the critical parameters of a given vector preparation that may be key to vector performance. This is exemplified by challenges in analyzing the impurities within AAV vector products such as defective viral particles that closely resemble the vector itself. The scientists of the proposed Molecular Virology Core (MVC) developed a series of new assays on AAV vectors which provide additional critical parameters to be analyzed for safety of gene therapy. This unprecedented depth of analysis will provide Projects 1, 2, and 3 with the knowledge of vector composition that they require to interpret the outcomes of gene transfer experiments and help develop safer vectors. The MVC will pursue the following Specific Aims: 1) Manufacturing of quality vectors to support all projects: For results between studies and projects to be comparable, identical standards of vector production need to be applied. The proposed manufacturing process will further eliminate variables, e.g., use of plasmid backbone-free production, among other innovations. In addition, MVC will aid Projects 1, 2 and 3 in vector development, incorporating new discoveries and generating novel AAV vectors that improve hepatic FVIII gene delivery. 2) Providing in-depth molecular characterization of AAV vectors for in vitro and in vivo studies: MVC will provide single AAV genome analysis using a newly developed assay based on PacBio sequencing and bioinformatic analysis of the sequence data. Traditional AAV vector assays such as AAV titering by ELISA, Southern blot analysis, silver staining as well as digital PCR/qPCR will also be performed. 3) In-depth analysis for AAV genome status post-delivery. AAV genomes status in vivo will be analyzed by next generation sequencing as well as traditional Southern blot and qPCR. AAV transcriptome analysis will also be included.

title: Innate immune responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection in the olfactory epithelium
text:
Olfactory loss is reported as an early symptom and predictor for COVID-19. The supporting sustentacular
cells but not the olfactory sensory neurons in the olfactory epithelium are permissive for SARS-CoV-2
infection. The goal of this proposal is to better understand the innate responses in sustentacular cells upon
SARS-CoV-2 infection and how these responses contribute to olfactory dysfunction.

title: Novel Mechanisms in Adenoviral Ocular Pathogenesis
text:
Adenovirus is the most common cause of human eye infection, and yet at present there is no
effective therapy. We will study adenovirus pathogenesis in the three major ocular surface
epithelial cell types with a specific focus on host/pathogen protein interactions relevant to the
hyperinflammatory condition known as epidemic keratoconjunctivitis. In the absence of an FDA-
approved therapy for adenovirus infection, studies on fundamental mechanisms of host/pathogen
interactions in the nucleus and cytoplasm of adenovirus infected ocular surface epithelium may
lead to a novel but effective antiviral therapy.

title: Enabling high-fidelity population voltage imaging with next-generation optical platforms and indicators
text:
Genetically encoded voltage indicators (GEVIs) have recently emerged as powerful optical tools for capturing
neuronal electrical activity with genetic specificity in a high-throughput manner, which is critical for
understanding how complex brain functions in mammals arise from parallel and distributed neural
computations. However, the fast temporal dynamics, low brightness, and limited sensitivity of GEVIs, coupled
with a lack optical systems designed in a principled manner based on intrinsic GEVI properties, have prevented
the full exploitation of their potential. In this project, we propose an integrated approach that combines the
engineering of enhanced GEVIs with the design, implementation, and application of advanced optical imaging
technologies.

title: Deciphering and Targeting Epigenetic Accessory Proteins in Acute myeloid Leukemia
text:
Acute myeloid leukemia is an aggressive blood cancer that affects more than 20,000 Americans each year, and
many patients still lack effective targeted therapies. This project identifies the epigenetic accessory protein
JADE2 as a new potential therapeutic target and investigates its role in regulating gene expression, driving
leukemia progression, and influencing treatment response. The findings will uncover key disease mechanisms
and guide the development of more effective targeted therapies to improve outcomes for people with leukemia.

title: The NYU-Sage NAMs Data Hub and Coordinating Center: Harmonizing, Analyzing, and Disseminating New-Approach-Methodologies Data
text:
As part of the Complement-ARIE program, the NYU-Sage New Approach Methodologies (NAMs) Data Hub
and Coordinating Center will create a controlled access platform for researchers to share and analyze data
from NAMs approaches. We will build tools to standardize and harmonize NAMs data, store it securely, and
provide researchers with powerful analytical and visualization tools. This will accelerate NAMs adoption,
reduce animal testing, and speed biomedical discovery.

title: Training Program in Chronobiology, Sleep and Sleep Disorders
text:
This training program provides state-of-the-art research training for PhD, MD, VMD, and MD/PhD
postdoctoral fellows in sleep and circadian research. The program is built on a combination of relevant didactic
training with individualized mentored research training. The program includes specific tracks for basic research,
clinical/translational research, and development of personalized medicine.

title: Discovery, Biosynthesis and Engineering of Side-Chain-Macrocyclic Plant Peptides
text:
Plant natural products are the source of ~25% of FDA-approved drugs but drug discovery and development from
plants is challenging due to rediscovery of known compounds and difficult scaled production and diversification
of lead structures. To overcome these bottlenecks, the proposed research will develop a gene-guided approach
to systematically discover new cyclic peptide natural products from plants by (a) mining plant genomes for new
peptide biosynthetic genes, (b) biosynthesis of plant peptide lead structures via new plant peptide cyclases and
(c) production of plant peptide libraries from diversified plant peptide precursor genes. Cyclic plant peptides are
an attractive test case for gene-guided discovery of plant natural product drugs as they constitute lead structures
for antiviral and anticancer therapy due to high oral bioavailability, stability and target specificity.

title: Plasticity and social neuromodulation of developing auditory cortical circuits
text:
Postnatal development involves significant experience-dependent neuroplasticity as well as heightened reliance
upon other individuals for caregiving. Developmental plasticity of the auditory cortex shapes lifelong perception,
such as for vocal signals like human language, but how cellular, neuromodulatory, and environmental factors
interact to orchestrate this plasticity is unclear. The proposed research utilizes novel methods for longitudinal
monitoring of neuronal cell-types and neuromodulatory inputs in the developing auditory cortex to test the
hypothesis that neuromodulation of developing inhibitory circuits regulates experience-dependent auditory
cortical plasticity in a social context-dependent manner.

title: Improving Microbiome Science by Modeling the Measurement Process
text:
The development of modern high-throughput methods that can measure entire microbial communities has
changed our understanding of the human microbiome and its effect on our health and well-being, but gaps and
shortcomings in these measurement methods remain a major impediment. This research will develop new
computational models and methods that will help scientists and health professionals accurately measure
microbiomes in the many sites in the human body where they reside. Better measurement of the human
microbiome will speed progress towards new diagnostics and treatments for health conditions related to the
human microbiome.

title: Uncovering Non-canonical Roles of Phosphagen Systems in Stress Resilience Using C. elegans
text:
This research aims to establish how an important class of enzymes, phosphagen kinases,
support responses to cellular stress through previously unknown or unappreciated functions.
Our work will pave the way for novel aging and disease interventions involving these enzymes
and provide many opportunities for student training and engagement, fostering the next
generation of scientists and America’s continued superiority in biomedical research.

title: Elucidating Context-Specific FERONIA Receptor Kinase Signaling
text:
Elucidating Context-Specific FERONIA Receptor Kinase Signaling
Project Narrative
The proposed studies will provide unprecedent new insights into how FER receptor kinase
achieves signaling specificity. Receptor kinases signaling pathways play critical roles in diverse
cellular processes and deregulation of the pathways leads to serious human diseases such as
cancer. Understanding the pathway specificity has been a major area of study in developing
effective therapies. Better understanding cell signaling specificity of FER receptor kinase can
help shed light on receptor kinase signaling pathways related to human health.
